text.p: Vontobel Group, the Swiss-based bank specialised in financial asset management, said results continued to show an increase in the first quarter of 1997, after earnings rose in 1996.

"The business showed a promising trend in the first quarter of 1997. Income from both commissions and trading were higher at the end of March than the comparable levels of the previous year," Chief Executive Officer Hans-Dieter Vontobel said in the company's annual report.

"The Vontobel Group's results for the first quarter of 1997 are very good. As (per) the end of March, all income items were substantially above budget and previous year's figures," the group said in a text presented with its annual earnings.
The bank reported already in February that its group net rose 47 percent to 60.2 million Swiss francs in 1996 from 41.1 million in 1995, excluding minorities.
It also said it was raising its dividend to 25 francs per bearer share from 22 francs and to 5.00 francs from 4.40 francs per registered share.

Elaborating on expectations for the rest of 1997, Vontobel said at a news briefing that its outlook could be affected by markets, but the performance in the first quarter was based on conservative management.

"Of course, it (the 1997 result) depends on markets. But it is not the case that we had to throw everything on the table in the first quarter in order to make this statement (of higher results). Certainly, if financial markets tend sideways or experience further declines, it will have a certain impact. We have reckoned with that for quite a while," Vontobel said.
In its annual report, it noted that extraordinary expenditures included a 22.9 million Swiss franc allocation to reserves, which compared with 700,000 francs in 1995 in the same slot last year.
Asked whether the allocation was aimed more at providing for risk, or was intended to smooth out results, Vontobel said the decision reflected elements of both.
"Of course we have more assets, we have more volume, we have more products," he said.
"One cannot ignore the fact that with rising volume and complexity, it makes sense to add to reserves," Vontobel said.
Assets under management rose to 35.7 billion Swiss francs in 1996 from 24.5 billion in 1995. The increase was fairly evenly split between new inflows and performance-related gains.
